etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English utmost, utemest [and other forms], from Old English ūtmest, ūtemest [and other forms], from ūt, ūte (“out; outdoors, outside”) + -mest (suffix meaning ‘furthest’, used to form superlatives of some adjectives) (and conflated with most). Ūt is derived from Proto-Germanic *ūt (“out, outward”), from Proto-Indo-European *úd (“out, outward”). Equivalent to out +‎ -most.

definitions.definition: Situated at the most distant limit; farthest, outermost.

quote.citation: [1633], George Herbert, “The Sacrifice”, in [Nicholas Ferrar], editor, The Temple. Sacred Poems, and Private Ejaculations, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire:  […]  Thomas Buck and Roger Daniel; and are to be sold by Francis Green, […], →OCLC, page 26:

definitions.definition: The greatest possible capability, extent, or quantity; maximum.
